stories.headline: As the flag unfurls
stories.title: As the flag unfurls
stories.summary: As Prime Minister Narendra Modi unfurls the national flag on India’s 80th Independence Day on the ramparts of the fort that Shahjahan built he would be acutely aware of the very difficult external environment that confronts the nation. The Iran war continues causing continuing dislocation in international energy supplies. This has impacted India directly because it had depended on both oil and gas supplies from the Gulf region. India has successfully made arrangements to ensure that there were no long term shortages of fuel or fertilizers but their costs have increased putting pressure on the economy. The Ukraine war has gone beyond four years now and while its principal impact is being felt in Europe it has added tension to the relations of the Great Powers and this in turn affects the international community as well. While these major conflicts are playing out the principal global contention of the present age is between China which has risen to great power status and the United States which remains the most powerful country in the world. However, the gap between them is narrowing. These factors require that India’s foreign policy and security managers handle India’s external relations with subtlety and dexterity to ensure that national interests are safeguarded and promoted. What makes the situation more complex is that these contestations are occurring at a time of great scientific and technological change. The world is in the midst of the Fourth Industrial Revolution. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has begun to impact all aspects of human life. If the countries where the First Industrial Revolution occurred from the mid-19th century prospered and became powerful, now it will be those that would be in the forefront of the Fourth Industrial Revolution.. The current leading states in the field of AI are the US and China. It is in them that basic research in the AI area is taking place. Others are handling the applications that are emerging from this fundamental research and development. India too is attempting to gain ground in the applications area but the challenge is to undertake basic R&D. It is good that for this purpose the government has set up The National Research Foundation and allocated Rs one lakh crore to it. It is essential that this Foundation ensures that India is able to make strides in the development of fundamental S&T in all areas of the current Industrial Revolution and looks beyond that too. External challenges in the midst of the radical S&T transformations underway require internal cohesion and social harmony. Indeed social peace is a strategic asset whose value cannot be over emphasised. As the country is making strides under the present government ideological and political differences have also emerged. It is the responsibility of the political class to ensure that their differing viewpoints which are natural in a democracy are so managed that they do not impinge on national security. There is little doubt that the Constitution is the best guide for the management of all aspects of India’s national life. It is a living document which is capable of ensuring that the aspirations of all sections of the people are met. Its inclusive values ensure justice and equity even as the public culture of the country changes. Public culture too is never static. It reflects the times but what is important is that even while it changes it does not impinge on the sentiments of different sections of Indian society. India’s population is around one-sixth of that of the world. That makes the management of social change not an easy task for those who lead the country. On the 80th Independence Day the country can take satisfaction at its enormous economic progress which has taken it to the forefront of global economies. The rate of poverty has fallen and famines which occurred before independence are now a matter of history. The Indian farmer through his hard work has ensured self-sufficiency in almost all kinds of agricultural production. This is an undoubted achievement. But manufacturing is lagging behind and its pace has to quicken to ensure employment. Above all the constitution emphasises in Article 39 which is a part of the Directive Principles of State Policy that the economic system of the country should not result in the concentration of wealth. It therefore cautions against great disparities in wealth and income. This does not mean that economic activity should be stifled or the old modes of economic order which had outlived their utility should be revived but the constitution’s advice provides for social stability which is essential at all times but especially in one which is full of great external challenges emanating from the region and beyond. Anniversaries of national days are also a time for reflection not only for governments but for all citizens. As this writer considers India’s present situation he, like many other citizens, considers that two areas require the special attention of the state. These are education and health. They require far greater state participation than there is at present. They simply cannot be reduced to businesses. All this stated it has to be asserted that the security of the state is of paramount importance. It has to be secured in a rapidly changing environment where modes of regular and irregular war-fighting are undergoing great transformation. There is no doubt that India’s security forces are capable of defending the country and have the ability and agility to respond to these new challenges.

stories.headline: Trump administration asks US Supreme Court to allow White House ballroom work
stories.title: Trump administration asks US Supreme Court to allow White House ballroom work
stories.summary: The Trump administration has asked the US Supreme Court to allow construction of a USD 400 million White House ballroom to continue while it appeals a lower court order halting aboveground work, arguing the project is essential for national security
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

event term: 'national security' in summary weight 42
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: Washington: President Donald Trump’s administration on Friday asked the US Supreme Court to allow the White House to continue construction on its USD 400 million ballroom project while it appeals a lower court’s order to halt the work.
Trump’s solicitor general petitioned the high court to suspend last week’s decision by a three-judge panel from the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.
Chief Justice John Roberts set a deadline of Tuesday for a response by plaintiffs challenging the ballroom project.
The divided appeals court panel ruled last week Trump must stop the White House ballroom’s construction because Congress has not approved the project.

The panel’s majority said Trump doesn’t have the unilateral authority to build a 90,000-square-foot (8,400-square-metre) ballroom where the White House’s East Wing stood before he ordered its demolition last fall.
The lower court suspended its own ruling for two weeks to give Trump’s Republican administration time to appeal to the Supreme Court.
Solicitor General D John Sauer asked the Supreme Court to rule on its stay petition before the appeals court panel’s decision takes effect on August 21.

“This case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security,” Sauer wrote.
In April, a district court judge ordered a stop to aboveground construction of the planned ballroom.
But the judge stressed that the White House was free to proceed with underground work, including the construction of any bunkers, military installations and medical facilities.
The DC Circuit panel’s 2-1 decision upheld an order to pause aboveground construction on the project, siding with historic preservationists who sued to stop construction of the ballroom.

“Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help,” wrote the majority’s two judges, both appointed by Democratic presidents.

stories.headline: India at 80
stories.title: India at 80
stories.summary: On 15 August 2026, India will mark its 80th Independence Day. The occasion should not be limited to remembering the end of British rule. It should also make us ask a basic question: what does freedom mean in the actual lives of Indian citizens? India became politically independent in 1947, and the Constitution came into force in 1950. Its Preamble promises justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. These principles are not ceremonial words. They are the standards by which the Republic should judge its own progress. India’s democratic achievement is significant. It adopted universal adult franchise from the beginning of the Republic and has maintained regular elections despite deep differences of religion, language, caste, region and economic condition. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, voter turnout was 66.10 per cent. Women constituted 48.62 per cent of registered electors, and their turnout was 65.78 per cent, compared with 65.55 per cent for men. These figures show strong participation. But democracy is more than voting. It also requires equal rights, accountable institutions and the freedom to question those who exercise public power. The Constitution provides the foundation for these rights. Article 14 guarantees equality before law. Article 15 prohibits discrimination on specified grounds, including religion, race, caste and sex. Article 19 protects important freedoms, including speech and expression. Article 21 protects life and personal liberty. These provisions establish a clear principle: the State must respect the rights and dignity of every citizen. Yet legal equality does not automatically create social equality. B.R. Ambedkar examined this problem in Annihilation of Caste. He argued that political democracy cannot survive when social relations deny equality. In The Buddha and His Dhamma, he placed liberty, equality and fraternity at the centre of social life. The Constitution itself recognises the problem of inequality. Article 38 directs the State to reduce inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities. Article 39 calls for adequate means of livelihood and seeks to prevent excessive concentration of wealth. India has made major economic progress. The World Bank reports that since 2000 India’s economy has nearly quadrupled in real terms, while real per-capita income has almost tripled. The IMF projects 7.0 per cent real GDP growth in 2026. These achievements matter. But GDP growth is not the same as human development. Growth becomes meaningful when it creates secure work, raises incomes and improves education, healthcare and living conditions. India has also reduced poverty. But poverty cannot be understood only through an income threshold. A family may move above a poverty line and still face poor housing, inadequate healthcare, weak education or insecure employment. Employment is therefore a central test of economic freedom. The PLFS 2025 recorded labour-force participation of 59.3 per cent among people aged 15 years and above. The rate was 79.1 per cent for men and only 40.0 per cent for women. This gap is a serious equality issue. Women need equal access to paid work and public decision-making. Constitutional equality must be visible in people’s actual opportunities, not only in legal provisions. Gandhi’s Hind Swaraj gives freedom a wider meaning. For Gandhi, swaraj was not simply the replacement of British rulers by Indian rulers. It also required self-rule, personal responsibility, social cooperation and moral discipline. Political independence was therefore the beginning of freedom, not its completion. Education is equally important. Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen, while Article 51A(h) asks citizens to develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform. Education should enable citizens to examine evidence, question false claims and disagree peacefully. Without these abilities, the right to vote cannot by itself create a strong democracy. Rabindranath Tagore’s Nationalism offers another important warning. Tagore opposed nationalism when political power was placed above human dignity. His vision of a society “where the mind is without fear” remains relevant. Legal freedom is incomplete when people live under fear caused by poverty, discrimination, violence or arbitrary power. Human development provides another measure of progress. The UNDP Human Development Report 2025 ranked India 130th among 193 countries, with an HDI of 0.685 for 2023. The report estimates that inequality reduces India’s HDI by 30.7 per cent. The lesson is direct: national income matters, but health, education and living standards matter equally. Fraternity is another essential part of freedom. Article 51A(e) asks citizens to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood. India contains many religions, languages, castes and regional identities. These differences do not threaten national unity when all citizens receive equal constitutional protection. National unity should be based on equal citizenship, not social uniformity. Environmental protection is also connected with human freedom. Article 48A directs the State to protect and improve the environment, while Article 51A(g) places an environmental duty on citizens. Clean air, safe water and a healthy environment are basic conditions of a dignified life. India now looks towards 2047, the centenary of Independence. The goal should be precise. Development should provide equal educational opportunities, dignified employment, accessible healthcare, greater participation of women, accountable institutions and equal protection of law. Ambedkar taught that political equality requires social equality. Gandhi connected freedom with swaraj and responsibility. Tagore connected freedom with reason and freedom from fear. Their ideas remain relevant because political independence alone cannot guarantee human freedom. At 80, India should celebrate what it has achieved, but it should also confront what remains unfinished. Independence freed India from colonial rule. The Constitution demands freedom, equality and dignity for its people. The real test is whether that promise is lived by every citizen. Dr. Sabzar Ahmad Bhat, PhD, Central University of Gujarat.
